14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Romans 14–15 address a specific pastoral conflict in the Roman church: tension between Jewish Christians who maintained food laws and Sabbath observances ("the weak in faith") and Gentile Christians who felt free from such regulations ("the strong"). But Paul's treatment of this specific conflict generates principles that apply to every generation's version of the same tension: the conflict between Christian liberty and Christian love, between what I am free to do and what love requires me to do for the sake of my brother.

The governing principle is not the extension of legal restriction to those who are free, nor the dismissal of sensitive consciences as mere scrupulosity. It is love — the willingness to limit one's own legitimate freedom for the sake of the weaker brother's conscience and the unity of the body. Paul himself is clearly among "the strong" (15:1 — "we who are strong"), but his pastoral concern is to protect the weak while educating them toward greater freedom, without allowing either group to destroy the other with contempt or judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions" (v. 1). The command is striking in both its positive and its negative dimensions. Positively: welcome him — bring him into the full fellowship of the community, do not treat his scruples as a reason for exclusion. Negatively: not to quarrel over opinions — do not make his welcome the occasion for pressuring him to adopt your view or defend your freedom. The welcome is genuine; the agenda of the welcome is his good, not your point-scoring.

The specific examples Paul uses — one person eats only vegetables, another observes certain days as special — are illustrations of a broader principle. The particulars may be first-century Jewish food laws and Sabbath observances; the principle is the obligation of both the strong and the weak to refrain from the two characteristic sins their positions generate: the strong's temptation to despise the scrupulous (treating their sensitivity as weakness or intellectual failure), and the weak's temptation to judge the free (condemning as sinful what God has declared clean).

"Each of us will give an account of himself to God" (v. 12) — the eschatological horizon is the great leveller. Neither the strong nor the weak will stand before God and be assessed on the basis of whether they were free in matters of food and days. They will give an account of themselves — whether they served Christ, whether they loved their brother, whether they built up the body. The things that divide them now will be irrelevant then; what will matter then should be what governs them now.

Four things in the section are worth adding, because the ground between the opening command and v. 12 is where the argument is actually made. The first is v. 4, which supplies the reason judging is out of order: Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? The picture is a domestic household. You do not discipline another man’s staff, however sure you are that they are doing it wrong, because they were not hired by you and do not answer to you.

And that verse ends in a promise rather than a rebuke — he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. Paul’s confidence is not that the disputed practice does not matter but that the disputed brother is being personally held up by someone competent. God is already at work on the person you were about to correct.

The second is v. 6, and it is the criterion the whole section turns on. Both parties — the one who observes the day and the one who does not, the one who eats and the one who abstains — are described as acting in honour of the Lord, and both are said to give thanks to God. Paul is not calling the difference trivial. He is pointing out that the same thanksgiving is going up from both sides of the table.

The third is v. 9, which grounds the whole thing in the gospel rather than in tolerance: to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. The purpose of the cross and resurrection is stated here as lordship — which settles who is entitled to rule another believer’s conscience, and the answer is the one who paid for it. And the fourth is vv. 10–11, where the argument is sealed with Isaiah 45:23: every knee bowing, every tongue confessing, the strong and the weak side by side at the same tribunal, neither of them presiding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adiaphora and the Conscience

The Reformed tradition uses the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor prohibits — the territory of Romans 14. In these matters, Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean; what the gospel has freed the conscience from need not be re-enslaved. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that in matters of adiaphora, the strong must exercise their freedom with sensitivity to the weaker conscience — not capitulating to every scruple indefinitely, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific tensions in Rome were between Jewish and Gentile believers over Torah food laws and calendar observances — real, living issues that threatened the unity of a church in which both groups worshipped together. Paul does not resolve the tension by declaring one group right and the other wrong; he transcends it by pointing both groups to a standard higher than their own position: the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation of the church has its equivalent of the Romans 14 debate: alcohol, entertainment, dress, worship style, political engagement. The principles are the same: welcome the brother with differing scruples; do not quarrel over opinions; do not despise; do not judge; remember that each will give account to God and not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church must welcome believers with tender consciences, without turning disputed matters into quarrels.

Weak in faith. Not weak in trusting Christ, but not yet fully persuaded of the freedom the gospel gives in matters like food.

Welcome him. The same word as 15:7: as Christ welcomed you.

Opinions. Paul is dealing with disputable matters, not the gospel itself. On the gospel he does not compromise (Galatians 1:8).

On a Tuesday. Welcome the Christian whose scruples you find tiresome, without trying to win the argument.
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither the free nor the scrupulous may look down on or judge the other, for God has accepted both, and each answers to his own Master.

Two sins. The strong are tempted to despise; the weak are tempted to judge.

Another’s servant. You are not your fellow believer’s master. Christ is.

He will be upheld. The Lord is able to make his servant stand. A gentle word of perseverance.

On a Tuesday. Notice whether your reaction to a different Christian is contempt or condemnation, and drop both.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some esteem certain days as special and others treat all days alike; each should be fully convinced and act in honour of the Lord.

The days. Most likely the Jewish Sabbath, feasts and fasts.

Fully convinced. Act from conviction, not imitation or pressure.

Where Christians differ: does this include the Lord’s Day? Sabbatarians (the Westminster tradition) argue that Paul is speaking of Jewish ceremonial days only, and that the fourth commandment continues in the Christian Sunday. Others read it more widely: no day is binding on the Christian conscience. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), so its rules do not bind the Christian conscience. Yet the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a privilege to be received gladly: a day for gathered worship and rest. Hold the view charitably.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add, “the one who does not observe the day, does not observe it in honor of the Lord.” It is a natural expansion; the earliest manuscripts lack it.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you do with your days, do it for the Lord with thanks.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No believer lives or dies for himself; in life and in death, we belong to the Lord.

Not to himself. Not a statement about our social nature, but about whose we are.

We are the Lord’s. Compare the first answer of the Heidelberg Catechism: our only comfort is that we belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to our faithful Saviour.

For worship. Rest in this: whatever happens today, you are his.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ died and rose to be Lord of both the dead and the living.

Died and lived again. The cross and the resurrection won his lordship (Philippians 2:8–11).

Lord of the dead. Believers who have died are not beyond his care.

On a Tuesday. If Christ is Lord of your brother, leave the judging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why judge or despise your brother, when all will stand before God’s judgment seat, where every knee will bow?

Your brother. The word Paul repeats. You are speaking of family.

The judgment seat. Believers are not condemned (8:1), yet they will give an account of their lives (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Isaiah 45:23. Every knee will bow to God. Philippians 2:10–11 applies the same text to Jesus.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “the judgment seat of Christ”, probably from 2 Corinthians 5:10. The earliest read “of God”.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each of us will give an account of himself to God.

Of himself. Not of your brother. You answer for your own life.

On a Tuesday. Spend more energy on your own account than on other people’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (v. 13). The second half of chapter 14 moves from the mutual prohibition of judging and despising to the positive obligation of the strong: limit your freedom in cases where exercising it would damage your brother's conscience and lead him into sin. The governing concern is his welfare, not your rights.

Paul's theological grounding of this obligation is striking: "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (v. 15). Christ died for the weak brother. The price paid for his soul is the blood of the Son of God. The strong believer who uses her freedom to demolish someone Christ purchased at infinite cost has committed something far more serious than poor table manners. She has treated as worthless what God treated as worth his Son.

The kingdom of God principle of v. 17 is the positive vision behind the self-limitation: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." The things that matter most — right standing before God, harmony in the body, Spirit-given joy — are not determined by what we eat. The strong person who surrenders her food freedom for the sake of a brother's peace and joy has not lost anything that matters; she has demonstrated something that matters supremely: she cares more about his joy in the Holy Spirit than about her right to eat what she pleases.

Verses 13, 15 and 17 carry the section, and the rest of it carries the argument. Verse 14 is the pivot, and it is the boldest sentence in the chapter: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Both halves are asserted. The thing really is clean, and it really is defiling for the man whose conscience says otherwise — which is why the answer to his scruple is teaching rather than pressure.

Verses 16 and 19–21 then supply the working rules. Do not let the good thing you possess — your liberty — get itself a bad name (v. 16). Pursue what makes for peace and for building up (v. 19). And the counterpart: do not, for the sake of food, demolish the work of God (v. 20). Paul is running a construction metaphor across these verses, and the choice he puts to the strong is whether their freedom is putting walls up or taking them down.

Verse 22 turns to the free man personally: the faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Not conceal your convictions, but stop parading a liberty — and then a beatitude for the man who can act without a backward glance at himself.

And v. 23 closes the chapter with the sentence that has travelled furthest from it: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. In context it is about a specific man doing a specific thing while divided in his own mind. It has been made to carry a great deal more than that.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian Liberty and the Law of Love

Romans 14:13–23 establishes the fundamental principle of Christian ethics in matters of liberty: freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is not a license to do everything the law permits without regard to others; it is the freedom to serve. The one who is free in Christ is freed from the bondage of sin and law — freed for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother's conscience is a misuse of freedom as fundamental as legalism; it is just as self-centred, only differently oriented.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific issue of meat offered to idols (closely related to the Romans 14 situation, developed more fully in 1 Corinthians 8–10) was a genuine and daily challenge in the first-century city. Much of the meat available in the marketplace had passed through a pagan temple. The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul's principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother's conscience. Now: The strong Christian in every age is tempted to treat her freedom as a badge of theological maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be managed with care. The test of genuine maturity is not the willingness to exercise freedom but the willingness to limit it out of love — to choose the brother's conscience over personal preference, his joy over your rights.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop judging one another and resolve never to put a stumbling block before a brother; nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean to the one who thinks it so.

A wordplay. Stop judging others; judge (decide) this instead: never trip a brother up.

Nothing unclean in itself. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Paul is persuaded in the Lord.

Unclean for him. Conscience matters. To act against it, even when it is mistaken, is to sin (v. 23).

What it does not mean. This is about things indifferent. Sin does not become acceptable because someone thinks it fine.

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If what you eat grieves your brother, you are not walking in love; do not destroy for the sake of food one for whom Christ died.

Grieved. Not merely annoyed, but wounded, drawn to act against his conscience.

For whom Christ died. If Christ gave his life for him, can you not give up a meal?

Where Christians differ: can a believer be destroyed? Some argue that this proves a person Christ died for can finally perish. Verdict: Paul is warning about the real damage our conduct can do, and judging by what we can see: he is a brother. God keeps his elect (8:30–39), and he does so in part through warnings like this. The verse does not undo definite atonement or perseverance, but it leaves no room for carelessness.

On a Tuesday. Is there a freedom you enjoy that you should lay aside for someone’s sake?

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your freedom be slandered, for God’s kingdom is not about food and drink but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

Your good. Christian liberty is good. Do not use it in a way that brings it into disrepute.

The kingdom. Food is not what matters: what matters is right standing and living, peace with God and each other, and Spirit-given joy.

On a Tuesday. Measure your church’s quarrels by this verse. Most turn out to be about eating and drinking.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever serves Christ in this way pleases God and is respected by people; so pursue what makes for peace and builds each other up.

Pursue. Peace is not passive. It must be chased.

Mutual upbuilding. Ask of every freedom: does it build the other up?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not tear down God’s work over food; all food is clean, but it is wrong to cause another to stumble, and good to give up meat or wine or anything that does.

The work of God. Your brother is God’s workmanship (Ephesians 2:10).

Where Christians differ: total abstinence. Some have used this verse to require all Christians to abstain from alcohol. Verdict: Scripture treats wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15; John 2) and condemns drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). Paul calls for willing, loving restraint in specific situations, not a universal rule. Abstinence is a good choice for some, and a loving one where it protects a brother, but it is not a test of faith.

On a Tuesday. Order your drink with the weakest person at the table in mind.

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your convictions about these matters between yourself and God; blessed is the one whose conscience does not condemn what he approves.

Keep it to yourself. Not concealing the truth, but not parading your freedom to unsettle others.

A clear conscience. A real blessing, worth more than any freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever eats while doubting is condemned, because the eating is not from faith, and whatever does not come from faith is sin.

Not from faith. Here faith means a confident conviction before God that an action is right.

Whatever does not proceed from faith. To act against conscience is sin, even if the act is harmless in itself.

What it does not mean. Not that conscience is infallible. A weak conscience should be taught by Scripture, but not bullied into acting before it is persuaded.

Textual note. Some manuscripts place the doxology of 16:25–27 here; others after 15:33; a few omit it. The letter may have circulated in more than one form, but the doxology is in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the end.

On a Tuesday. Do not press another believer to do what their conscience forbids.

For worship. Thank God for a gospel that frees the conscience, and for the patience to wait for one another.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.

14.text: <sup>1</sup>As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions.<sup>2</sup>One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.<sup>3</sup>Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.<sup>4</sup>Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.<sup>5</sup>One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind.<sup>6</sup>The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.<sup>7</sup>For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself.<sup>8</sup>For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord’s.<sup>9</sup>For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.<sup>10</sup>Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God;<sup>11</sup>for it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.”<sup>12</sup>So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother.<sup>14</sup>I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean.<sup>15</sup>For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.<sup>16</sup>So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil.<sup>17</sup>For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.<sup>18</sup>Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men.<sup>19</sup>So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.<sup>20</sup>Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats.<sup>21</sup>It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.<sup>22</sup>The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.<sup>23</sup>But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.

15.title: Unity, Hope, and the Mission of Paul
15.overview:
Romans 15 brings together three threads: the conclusion of the weak/strong argument (vv. 1–13), the personal explanation of Paul's apostolic mission (vv. 14–21), and his travel plans and prayer requests (vv. 22–33). The chapter is held together by the theme of the worldwide scope of the gospel — Christ's own example of self-giving (vv. 1–3), the Gentile mission as the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy (vv. 9–12), and Paul's ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named (vv. 20–21).

The opening section (vv. 1–13) concludes the argument of chapter 14 by pointing to Christ as the model of the strong bearing with the failings of the weak. Christ did not please himself (v. 3) — He endured the reproaches of others for their sake. The strong who follow his example are not making a heroic sacrifice; they are imitating their Lord. And the doxological prayer of vv. 5–6 and 13 frames the whole argument in worship: the God of endurance, encouragement, hope, and peace is the one who enables the unity for which Paul prays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Example of Christ and the God of Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves" (v. 1). Paul has waited until now to identify himself with the strong — and he identifies himself only to place the obligation of the strong front and centre. The strong do not have the right to demand that the weak keep up with them; they have the obligation to bear with the weak, to build them up, to serve their good. "Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up" (v. 2).

The model is Christ: "For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me'" (v. 3, quoting Psalm 69:9). The Son of God did not come to be served but to serve — to bear not only the sins of the weak but their reproaches, their insults, the consequences of their failure. The one who is most perfectly strong became the servant of all. The Christian who follows this pattern — bearing the burdens of others rather than asserting the rights of the free — is walking in the footsteps of the one who bore our ultimate burden at Calvary.

The doxological climax of the section (vv. 5–6, 13) frames the whole practical argument in prayer and worship. Paul's wish is not merely that the Roman Christians be nice to each other; it is that they glorify God together with one voice (v. 6) — the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, all singing the same praise to the same God. And the God of hope fills with all joy and peace in believing (v. 13) — not the meagre joy of people who have resolved their differences, but the overflowing joy of people who have been given hope by the Spirit.

Between the example of Christ and that benediction stand four more things, and they carry the argument to its conclusion. The first is v. 4, which explains why Paul has just settled a first-century dispute about food by quoting a psalm: whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. The Old Testament was written for the benefit of readers who did not yet exist, and its stated product is not information but hope.

The second is v. 7, and it is the summit of everything since 14:1: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. The same verb Paul used in 14:1 for receiving the weak, and in 14:3 of God receiving him, now appears a third time with Christ himself as the measure. The strong were told to welcome; here everyone is told to welcome everyone, on the pattern of a welcome none of them deserved.

The third is vv. 8–9, where Paul states how one Christ serves two peoples. He became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs — that is, to demonstrate God’s truthfulness — and he did it so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. The two halves are not symmetrical, and the asymmetry is the point: Israel receives a kept promise, the nations receive sheer mercy, and neither group has grounds to look down on the other.

The fourth is the chain of quotations in vv. 9–12, drawn deliberately from every part of the Hebrew Bible — the Law (Deuteronomy 32:43), the Writings (Psalm 18:49; Psalm 117:1) and the Prophets (Isaiah 11:10). Paul is not producing a proof text. He is showing that the inclusion of the nations was the settled expectation of the whole canon, and the chain ends on the word the benediction will pick up: in him will the Gentiles hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as the Model of Solidarity with the Weak

The Christological grounding of the strong's obligation in Romans 15:3 is one of Paul's most important ethical moves. Ethics derived from the example of Christ is not mere imitation-of-a-good-man moralism; it is participation in the pattern of the one who is Lord, whose servanthood was the shape of his sovereignty, whose self-giving is the source of the Christian's capacity for self-giving. When Paul says "bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2), the law of Christ is precisely this: the pattern of the one who bore what he did not owe so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" — was not an abstract aspiration. The Roman church had real divisions: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people from different social classes and national backgrounds. The one voice of praise was the visible, social miracle that would demonstrate to the watching city of Rome that something genuinely new had entered the world. Now: The unity of diverse believers in genuine, cross-cultural, cross-social worship is still the most powerful apologetic the church has available. A community of people who have every reason to be divided — by race, class, culture, education, politics — worshipping together with one voice glorifies the God whose gospel is the only power that creates such unity.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strong must bear with the weaknesses of the weak, seeking their neighbour’s good rather than their own pleasure.

We who are strong. Paul counts himself among them (14:14), and so takes on the greater obligation.

Bear with. Carry, not merely tolerate. Strength exists to lift others.

Please his neighbour. Not flattery or people-pleasing (Galatians 1:10), but seeking his real good: building him up.

On a Tuesday. Where can you use your strength to carry someone weaker rather than to get your way?

parallels.desc: bear one another’s burdens

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ did not please himself, but took on himself the insults aimed at God.

Psalm 69:9. David’s psalm of suffering for God’s sake, fulfilled in Christ’s passion.

The pattern. Paul’s ethics always return to the cross. If Christ bore reproach for us, we can bear inconvenience for one another.

For worship. Thank Christ who bore the reproach that was yours.

parallels.desc: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Old Testament was written to teach us, so that through endurance and the encouragement of Scripture we might have hope; and Paul prays that God would give them harmony.

For our instruction. The Old Testament is Christian Scripture (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Timothy 3:16).

Endurance, encouragement, hope. Scripture produces endurance and encouragement, and these produce hope.

The God of endurance. What Scripture gives, God gives: Scripture is his voice.

In accord with Christ. Harmony is not uniformity of opinion, but shared allegiance to Christ.

On a Tuesday. When hope runs low, go back to the Old Testament stories of God’s faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of harmony is united praise to God; therefore welcome one another as Christ welcomed you, to God’s glory.

One voice. Strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, singing together. Unity is for worship.

As Christ welcomed you. The measure and motive: Christ welcomed you while you were weak, ungodly and an enemy (5:6–10).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “welcomed us” instead of “welcomed you”. Both are well attested; the sense is the same.

On a Tuesday. Whom in your church are you slow to welcome?

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ became a servant to the Jews to confirm God’s promises to the patriarchs, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy.

A servant to the circumcised. Jesus was born a Jew and ministered chiefly to Israel (Matthew 15:24).

Truthfulness and mercy. To Israel, God proved faithful to his word. To the Gentiles, who had no promise, he showed sheer mercy.

Psalm 18:49. David praises God among the nations.

parallels.desc: I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again it says, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture repeatedly calls the Gentiles to rejoice with God’s people and praise the Lord.

Deuteronomy 32:43 and Psalm 117:1. From the Law and the Psalms. God always meant the nations to praise him.

With his people. Gentiles join Israel’s worship; they do not replace it.

For worship. Join the praise of all the nations.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always intended Gentiles to praise him.

parallels.desc: rejoice with him, O heavens
praise the LORD, all nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah foretold that the root of Jesse would rise to rule the nations, and the Gentiles would hope in him.

Isaiah 11:10. The promised son of David, ruling over more than Israel.

Law, Psalms and Prophets. Paul has quoted all three parts of the Old Testament. The Gentile mission was not an afterthought.

In him will the Gentiles hope. This prepares for v. 13.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line.

parallels.desc: the root of Jesse, of him shall the nations inquire

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace as they trust him, so that they overflow with hope by the Spirit’s power.

The God of hope. Hope is his gift and comes from his character.

In believing. Joy and peace come through ongoing trust, not through circumstances.

Abound. Not just enough hope to get by, but overflowing.

By the power of the Holy Spirit. Hope is not optimism by effort but the Spirit’s work.

For worship. Pray this verse for yourself and for a friend who is losing heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now turns from theology and pastoral exhortation to autobiography and travel plans — and the transition is less abrupt than it appears. His account of his apostolic ministry is itself a miniature theology of mission. He describes himself as a minister (leitourgos — a cultic, priestly term) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, performing the priestly service of the gospel of God, offering the Gentiles as an acceptable offering, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (v. 16). The mission to the Gentiles is not merely evangelistic strategy; it is priestly worship — the bringing of the nations as an offering to God.

The scope of Paul's completed mission (vv. 19–21) is staggering: from Jerusalem to Illyricum (modern-day Croatia), he has "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ." Not because every person has heard it but because he has planted the gospel in strategic centres throughout the eastern Mediterranean, from which the word can spread into every surrounding region. His ambition going forward is equally characteristic: not to build on another man's foundation, but to preach where Christ has not yet been named. The pioneer missionary impulse is written into the logic of the commission.

The prayer request of vv. 30–33 is one of the most moving passages in Paul's letters. He asks the Roman church to "strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf" — the word for "strive together" (sunagōnizomai) is an athletic term, contending alongside someone in a contest. Prayer is work, and Paul wants co-labourers in it. He asks for three things: deliverance from unbelievers in Judea, acceptance of his offering by the Jerusalem church, and the joy of reaching Rome. All three will be granted, none in the form he pictured; the Rome visit will happen, but in chains.

Two stretches of the section deserve adding. The first is how it opens (vv. 14–15). Having written the most demanding letter in the New Testament, Paul tells its recipients that he is satisfied about them — full of goodness, filled with knowledge, able to instruct one another — and that what he has written is offered by way of reminder. He does not present a word of it as news.

The second is vv. 22–29, which contains the two most concrete things in the chapter. One is Spain (v. 24): Paul is not looking for another province but for the western edge of the known world, and he is asking Rome to become the base that sends him there. This is why the letter exists in the form it does.

The other is the Jerusalem collection (vv. 25–28), a relief fund gathered from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul is in Corinth, he intends to go west, and he is about to travel east instead — at real personal risk — to deliver money. And he does not call it charity. He says the Gentiles owe it to them (v. 27): having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, they owe material ones back. The collection is the argument of chapters 9–11 converted into currency and carried some eight hundred miles in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as Priestly Worship

Romans 15:16 is one of the most theologically rich descriptions of apostolic mission in the New Testament. Paul images his Gentile mission as priestly service — the offering of the nations to God as a sacrifice acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Spirit. This means that evangelism is not merely a strategy for church growth or a duty to be discharged; it is an act of worship, the gathering of the nations to lay them as a living offering before the God who created and redeemed them. This priestly vision of mission has sustained every great missionary movement in the Reformed tradition, from Calvin's Geneva sending missionaries to France, to William Carey going to India, to the countless sent ones who have carried the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's completed mission from Jerusalem to Illyricum represents perhaps fifteen years of gruelling apostolic labour — multiple missionary journeys, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, cold and hunger. The nonchalance with which he refers to having "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel" in this vast region is the confidence of a man who has done what he was sent to do and is already looking at the next frontier. Now: The pioneer missionary impulse of v. 20 — to preach where Christ has not been named — remains the highest calling in the church's mission. There are still places, peoples, and communities where the name of Christ has not been proclaimed. The obligation Paul felt is the obligation the church still carries, until all nations have heard.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident in the Roman Christians’ goodness and knowledge, yet has written boldly to remind them, because of the grace God gave him.

Able to instruct one another. Mutual teaching is the normal life of a healthy church.

By way of reminder. Christians need to hear again what they already know.

Boldly. Paul’s authority is not his own; it is grace given to him.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise reminders of familiar truth. They are how faith stays alive.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul describes his work as a priestly ministry, offering the Gentiles to God as an acceptable offering made holy by the Spirit, and this is his only ground for pride.

Priestly service. A picture: the gospel is preached, and believing Gentiles are presented to God as a living offering (12:1).

Where Christians differ: a ministerial priesthood? Roman Catholic theology has sometimes used such language to support an ordained priesthood offering sacrifice. Verdict: Paul’s priestly language is a metaphor for gospel preaching. The only atoning sacrifice is Christ’s (Hebrews 10:10–14), and all believers are priests (1 Peter 2:9).

Sanctified by the Spirit. It is the Spirit, not ritual, that makes the offering holy.

Proud in Christ. Not self-congratulation, but joy in what Christ has done.
verseByVerse.note: Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God.

parallels.desc: they shall bring your brothers as an offering

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will speak only of what Christ has done through him to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word, deed, signs and the Spirit’s power, from Jerusalem to Illyricum.

What Christ has accomplished. Paul takes no credit; Christ is the worker.

Obedience. The obedience of faith (1:5).

Signs and wonders. Marks of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12).

Where Christians differ: signs and wonders today. Continuationists expect the same signs to accompany evangelism today. Verdict: these signs confirmed the apostolic message in the foundation-laying era (Hebrews 2:3–4). God still heals in answer to prayer, but the gospel’s power today lies in the Spirit working through the word. Hold the view charitably.

Fulfilled. Not that every person had heard, but that the foundation was laid in key centres across the region.

Textual note. Manuscripts vary: “the Spirit of God”, “the Holy Spirit”, or simply “the Spirit”. The meaning is the same.
verseByVerse.note: Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s ambition was to preach Christ where he had not been named, not building on another’s foundation, as Isaiah foresaw.

Pioneer. Paul’s calling was to go where no church existed.

Isaiah 52:15. From the passage about the Suffering Servant: those who had never been told will see.

What it does not mean. Not that building on others’ foundations is wrong; Apollos watered what Paul planted (1 Corinthians 3:6). It was Paul’s particular calling.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the places and peoples where Christ is still not named.

parallels.desc: that which has not been told them they see

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
His work in the east had kept him from visiting Rome, but now that it is complete, he hopes at last to come.

Hindered. Paul’s plans were subject to God’s timing (1:13).

No more room. The pioneer work is done; others can build.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hopes to visit Rome on his way to Spain, and to be helped by them on that journey.

Spain. The western end of the known world, with few Jewish communities. A bold vision.

Helped on my journey. The phrase means support with supplies and people. Part of Paul’s purpose in writing Romans was to win a base for mission.

Did he reach Spain? Uncertain. Clement of Rome, writing around AD 96, says Paul reached “the limit of the west”, which may mean Spain.

On a Tuesday. Support those going where you cannot go.
verseByVerse.note: Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul ever reached it is uncertain; early tradition says he did.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First, Paul must go to Jerusalem with a gift the churches of Macedonia and Achaia have collected for the poor believers there.

The collection. Years of Paul’s work went into it (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Pleased. The giving was glad, not grudging.

Contribution. Koinōnia: fellowship in practical form.
verseByVerse.note: The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem was a major project of Paul’s later ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentiles gave gladly and also owed it, because having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings they should share their material ones.

Pleased and owed. Free and glad, yet fitting and right.

Spiritual and material. The gospel came from Jerusalem. Gratitude takes practical form (1 Corinthians 9:11).

On a Tuesday. Whom do you owe spiritually? How might you show thanks in practical ways?

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the gift is delivered, Paul will come to Rome on the way to Spain, confident he will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.

Completed. Literally “sealed”: delivered safely and properly.

The fullness of the blessing. Paul came to Rome in chains (Acts 28), yet still in the fullness of blessing.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “of the gospel” (“the blessing of the gospel of Christ”). The shorter reading is earlier.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urges them to strive with him in prayer for his safety from unbelievers in Judea, and for his gift to be accepted by the Jerusalem believers.

Strive together. Prayer is a struggle, a shared wrestling (Colossians 4:12).

The love of the Spirit. The love the Spirit pours into hearts (5:5).

Two fears. Danger from opponents, and rejection by fellow believers. Unity between Jewish and Gentile believers was at stake.

Answered prayer. Paul was rescued, but by arrest. God answers in ways we do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Ask someone to pray for you specifically, and pray specifically for them.
verseByVerse.note: These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hopes to come to them with joy by God’s will and be refreshed among them, and he prays the God of peace will be with them.

By God’s will. Paul plans, but leaves the outcome with God (James 4:15).

Refreshed. Even the apostle needed the encouragement of fellowship.

The God of peace. After chapters on division and unity, a fitting title.

For worship. Pray the God of peace to be with your church this week.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves.<sup>2</sup>Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.<sup>3</sup>For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, “The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me.”<sup>4</sup>For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.<sup>5</sup>May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,<sup>6</sup>that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>7</sup>Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.<sup>8</sup>For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God’s truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs,<sup>9</sup>and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”<sup>10</sup>And again it says, “Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.”<sup>11</sup>And again, “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”<sup>12</sup>And again Isaiah says, “The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope.”<sup>13</sup>May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.<sup>14</sup>I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another.<sup>15</sup>But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God<sup>16</sup>to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.<sup>17</sup>In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.<sup>18</sup>For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience—by word and deed,<sup>19</sup>by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ;<sup>20</sup>and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation,<sup>21</sup>but as it is written, “Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.”<sup>22</sup>This is the reason why I have For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.<sup>28</sup>When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you.<sup>29</sup>I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.<sup>30</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf,<sup>31</sup>that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,<sup>32</sup>so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company.<sup>33</sup>May the God of peace be with you all.
